title: The translator
hookLine: Rinchen Zangpo, who traveled to India to bring back texts
carry: knowing the words, and living them

cards: A young man from western Tibet sets out on foot, heading west, over passes where the snow never quite leaves. He doesn't speak the language of the people he's going to. He doesn't have the books he's going for.

What he has is a question: what did the Buddha actually say, and what did the great teachers of India write about it? The only way to find out is to go, learn their language, and carry the answers home on his back.

teach.h: THE ROAD TO KASHMIR AND INDIA.
teach.b: Tradition says he was sent from western Tibet, where kings had begun calling the teaching back after the quiet years.

He went to Kashmir and northern India, studied Sanskrit, and sat with Indian teachers until he could read their books the way they read them. Then he came home with texts, and with teachers willing to come too.
The work itself was often not one person alone at a desk.

teach.h: A PANDITA AND A LOTSAWA, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: An Indian scholar, a pandita, and a Tibetan translator worked side by side: one knew the Sanskrit from the inside, the other knew how Tibetans would hear it.
Tibetans call a translator a lotsawa, and it became a title of honor. Rinchen Zangpo is remembered as the great translator. Why so careful?
A Buddhist word carries a whole teaching inside it. Get the word for emptiness slightly wrong, and a reader walks off in the wrong direction for years.
So the lotsawas tried to keep one Tibetan word for one Sanskrit word, so a reader in a far valley would meet the same teaching as a reader near the capital. Then a story.
Atisha arrived when Rinchen Zangpo was already old and well-known. A story is told that Atisha questioned him and found his learning enormous.
Then he asked how the translator put all of it into practice, at once, on the cushion. The old translator, the story goes, went quiet, and then went into retreat.
Knowing the words and living them are two different journeys.
He had made the first. The story says he began the second.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism, the great translators, the lotsawas, are remembered by name and honored as teachers, and Tibetan translations of Indian texts traditionally name the Indian scholar and the Tibetan translator who made them.

games.q: you're Rinchen Zangpo, old and well-known for your learning. Atisha asks how you put all of it into practice at once. what do you do?
o: go quiet, and go into retreat.
tell him translation is practice enough.
games.why: the story says the old translator went quiet and then into retreat: knowing the words and living them were two journeys.

practice: Pick one word that matters to you, kindness, patience or home, in another language you know, a grandparent's, a neighbor's, one from school; if none comes, take lotsawa, translator.
Say it silently on each out-breath, and notice that someone had to carry it across a border so you could hear it. Then let the word go and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The translator. A lotsawa like Rinchen Zangpo, who walked to India and brought the teaching back into Tibetan, one careful word at a time.

carryVoice: Your line: knowing the words, and living them. The old translator had one road behind him and one ahead. Day nine hundred thirty-seven, done.
